overview: This small board pairs an infrared LED with a phototransistor: the LED constantly emits IR light, and the phototransistor detects how much bounces back off a nearby object. An onboard comparator chip (usually an LM393) turns that analog reflection level into a simple digital HIGH/LOW signal — 'something is close' or 'nothing is close' — with a trimpot to adjust the sensitivity threshold. It's cheaper and simpler than an ultrasonic sensor but far less precise: it can't tell you how far away something is, only whether it's within an adjustable trigger range, and dark or light-absorbing surfaces can fool it into never triggering.
simpleSummary: A simple sensor that shines invisible light and detects if something is in front of it.

specifications.outputType: Digital (HIGH/LOW), threshold set by an onboard trimpot

pinMap.name: VCC
pinMap.function: Power input for the IR LED and comparator circuit.

pinMap.name: OUT
pinMap.function: Digital output — typically LOW when an obstacle is detected within range, HIGH otherwise (some modules invert this).
pinMap.gotcha: Dark, matte, or angled surfaces absorb/deflect the IR beam and can fail to trigger detection even at close range — don't rely on it for reliably detecting all obstacle types.

useCases.title: Simple obstacle-avoiding robot
useCases.scenario: Mount 2-3 around a robot's perimeter for cheap, fast binary obstacle detection.

useCases.title: Object-present trigger
useCases.scenario: Trigger an action (alarm, counter, gate) when any object comes within range.

oftenConfusedWith: HC-SR04 (measures actual distance, not just presence)
oftenUpgradedTo: HC-SR04 or Sharp GP2Y0A21 when actual distance measurement is needed instead of simple detection
